title: A Strong Finish in 2026
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston uses the story of Olympic runner Louis Zamperini to prompt an end-of-year review. Zamperini, a 17-year-old at the 1936 Berlin Games, gained weight on the Olympic buffet and finished eighth in the 5,000 metres, yet ran his final lap in about 56 seconds, a sprint so striking that Hitler asked to meet the "kid with the fast finish." Houston asks what drives someone to dig deepest after hope of winning has passed. He recalls a mentor's yearly question, "What would a strong finish look like for you this year?", and recommends setting aside thirty minutes of silence to answer it in writing. He reviews his own Life Plan against categories such as work, family, health, finances, spirituality, fun and friends, and asks friends for their answers. The piece closes by challenging readers to build a lifelong habit of strong finishes.
points: Ask yourself what a strong finish would look like this year, and write the answer down during thirty minutes of silence.
Review the goals you set in January against life accounts such as work, family, health, finances, spirituality, fun and friends.
Goals may stay the same by the fourth quarter or change, and an honest year-end check shows which.
Hearing friends' answers to the same question is a source of inspiration and accountability.
Zamperini's final-lap sprint shows that effort at the end of a race can matter even when the early result is poor.
quotes: However, despite the limitations of his much heavier physical body, the Torrance Tornado had something deep inside his mind and spirit that flipped on like a switch in his last lap.
At the very end of his race, he somehow managed to run his final lap in an astonishing 56 seconds.
What makes a person run their fastest when all hope of winning has passed?

He would typically ask me this around September each year, as a way to force me to reflect upon and being intentional about my life and goals for the year, and to stay focused on the things that matter most.

I always find myself inspired and challenged by the things my friends say, whether it be a commitment to their families, a final business milestone they hope to achieve, or keeping a spiritual discipline during the chaos of the holidays.
Sometimes I have the same goals at the end of the year, and sometimes things have changed by the fourth quarter.
It can be helpful to review typical life accounts such as work, family, health, finances, spirituality, fun, or friends.
